requirements.requirement: /etc/inventory/app.conf exists on node1 as the source-of-truth inventory config
requirements.summary: Executor created /etc/inventory/app.conf on node1 with inventory application settings and confirmed its content directly.

requirements.requirement: A mechanism exists that keeps node2's copy of the file synchronized with node1's copy
requirements.summary: An SSH-trust-backed rsync pull script was installed on node2 and a cron job scheduled every 5 minutes to run it. Manual invocation confirmed the file was copied and checksums matched on both nodes.

requirements.requirement: Changes to node1's file are automatically picked up on node2 within 15 minutes, with no manual intervention
requirements.summary: A live edit on node1 was picked up automatically by node2's cron-driven sync within about 2-3 minutes (log entry at 11:05:01 after an edit at 11:02:42), with matching md5sums confirmed on both nodes without manual triggering. This is well within the 15-minute bound.

requirements.requirement: Sync mechanism (cron job, SSH trust, script) continues to function after node restarts, since ongoing synchronization is the core deliverable
requirements.summary: Both nodes were rebooted individually with boot_id changes directly observed and cross-confirmed against the fixed after-prepare/after-executor lifecycle snapshots (node1: 8c28f3cd...->8e3a09cd..., node2: 54089086...->353ebb16...). After both reboots, crond/sshd were active, the crontab entry persisted, and a fresh edit to node1's file was automatically synced to node2 within ~4.5 minutes (log entry 11:15:01), with matching checksums confirmed on both nodes.

overall_summary: The executor established a source-of-truth config on node1 and a cron-driven rsync pull mechanism on node2 that reliably picks up changes well inside the 15-minute requirement, verified both before and after independently restarting each node with directly observed, cross-checked boot-identity changes and post-restart recovery of the sync mechanism. All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct, corroborated evidence.
limitations: Two background 'wait for cron' helper processes (nohup sleep 320) failed to produce their intended output files, suggesting the background-process technique itself was unreliable in this environment; the executor worked around this with foreground sleeps instead, so final conclusions are not undermined, but the trace shows some wasted effort.
A small /tmp/reboot.log residue was left on both nodes after the reboot mechanism ran; this is trivial but was not explicitly cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Setup actions (SSH keys, /etc/hosts entries, cron job, script) are all necessary prerequisites for the sync mechanism and were not excessive. Two backgrounded 'nohup sleep 320' evidence-collection workarounds for a proxy timeout (cmd-2018a015081d4822, cmd-2e0c0f197a844cb5) never produced their intended log files and were effectively abandoned troubleshooting attempts; they were subsequently cleaned up via a matching pkill (cmd-d2b40961ed6b43f8), so no lingering process remained, though this reflects some inefficiency. A minor residual artifact, /tmp/reboot.log on both nodes (created by the reboot-scheduling nohup wrapper cmd-f6eeb101fadc4e94 and cmd-b2ed1ea3670f4496), was left behind and appears in the after-executor temporary-files diff without being cleaned up; this is low-risk residue (a small log file) but was not reverted.
